blocks.text: Plug a phone charger into a wall socket while PHCN is on, and a current of a fraction of an ampere trickles into the battery. Fire a petrol generator for the fridge and the current jumps to several amperes. Same copper wires, same idea: charge is flowing, and the size of that flow is what the electrician's meter is reading.

blocks.markdown:
**Electric current** $I$ is the rate of flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit:

$$I = \frac{Q}{t} \quad \text{or} \quad Q = It$$

The SI unit of current is the **ampere** (A): one ampere is a flow of one coulomb per second. Conventional current is drawn from the **positive** terminal of a cell towards the **negative** terminal, even though the electrons themselves drift the other way.

**Potential difference** (p.d.) $V$ between two points is the work done in moving one coulomb of charge from one point to the other. Its unit is the **volt** (V).

blocks.title: Ohm's law
blocks.text: Provided the temperature is constant, the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends. In symbols, V = IR, so the graph of I against V is a straight line through the origin. The constant R is the resistance of the conductor, measured in ohms (Ω).

blocks.title: Charge, current and resistance of a wire
blocks.prompt: A current of 2.5 A flows through a copper wire for 4.0 minutes. The wire is 2.0 m long, has cross-sectional area $0.40\ \text{mm}^2$ and resistivity $1.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m}$. Calculate (a) the charge that passes a point in the wire, (b) the resistance of the wire.

steps.text: (a) Convert the time to seconds and use Q = It.
(b) Convert the area to square metres.

items: Ammeter: always connected in series so that the whole current being measured passes through it. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.
Voltmeter: always connected in parallel with the component whose p.d. you want. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
Ohmic test: plot I against V (or V against I). A straight line through the origin at constant temperature means the conductor is ohmic.
Temperature: metals increase in resistance as they get hotter; that is why a lamp filament is non-ohmic once it glows.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Convert minutes to seconds before using Q = It. Convert mm² to m² (multiply by 10⁻⁶) before using R = ρl/A. On an I–V graph, resistance is the reciprocal of the gradient if I is plotted on the vertical axis; do not quote a gradient from a curve as if R were constant.

points: Current I = Q/t is the rate of flow of charge; 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹. Conventional current leaves the positive terminal of a cell.
Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature. The I–V graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin.
A filament lamp and a diode are non-ohmic: the lamp's resistance rises as it heats, and the diode conducts in one direction only.
Resistance of a wire: R = ρl/A, with ρ in Ω m, l in metres and A in square metres.
Ammeters go in series; voltmeters go in parallel.
